# How to Build a Clean Invoice and Payment Tracker in Excel with Copilot

> **In short:** You can use Copilot in Excel to build an invoice tracker by asking it in plain English to create columns, write formulas, and color overdue rows — but Copilot requires a paid Microsoft 365 plan, and it can't send reminder emails on its own.

If you send invoices to clients, you know the awkward feeling of chasing payments. A clean tracker turns that into a 30-second glance. With Copilot in Excel, you describe what you want in everyday words and watch a working tracker appear — no manual formula-writing, no fiddly formatting. This guide is for small-business owners, freelancers, and anyone who wants a simple "who owes me, and how late" view without buying accounting software.

## Before you start
- A paid Microsoft 365 subscription that includes Copilot (Copilot Pro for personal use, or Copilot for Microsoft 365 for business). Check Microsoft's official pricing page for the current plans and what's included.
- Excel on Windows, Mac, or the web. Some Copilot features vary slightly between desktop and web.
- About 15–20 minutes for the first build; faster once you have a template.
- A handful of real invoices to type in (even three to five rows is enough to test the formulas).

## Step 1 — Open a blank workbook and turn on Copilot
Open Excel and choose **Blank workbook**. Along the top, look for the **Home** tab and find the **Copilot** button at the right end of the ribbon — usually marked with a small sparkle ✨ icon. Click it once. A **chat panel slides open on the right side** of the screen with a welcome message and a few suggested prompts. If you don't see a Copilot button, your Microsoft 365 plan almost certainly doesn't include Copilot — that's the most common reason this step fails. As a fallback, scan the Home tab for any button labeled "Copilot", or check **File → Account** to confirm which plan you have.
💬 Example: in the panel, type "What can you do?" just to confirm it's working.
You'll know it worked when the chat panel appears on the right and Copilot replies to your first message.

## Step 2 — Ask Copilot to design the table
Click into cell **A1** so Copilot knows where to put the table. In the chat panel, type a request describing the columns you want. Copilot usually proposes a sample table and asks if you want to insert it — confirm and the column headers appear across row 1, with one row of example data in row 2. If your version refuses because the sheet is empty, just type one fake invoice in row 2 first and try the prompt again.
💬 Example: "Create a table with columns: Client, Invoice Number, Invoice Date, Due Date, Amount, Status, Days Overdue."
You'll know it worked when seven column headers appear in row 1, formatted as a table with small filter dropdown arrows on each header.

## Step 3 — Type in your real invoices (Status is a manual label)
Click into the first empty cell under each header and type your real invoice details — one invoice per row. Excel stores dates correctly when you include the year (like **15 March 2026** or **3/15/2026**), and amounts as numbers when you type just the digits. For the **Status** column, type a short label — **"Paid"**, **"Pending"**, or **"Overdue"**. You update these yourself as payments arrive; Status is a manual note, not a formula Copilot will calculate. If the filter dropdowns didn't appear after Step 2, click anywhere in your data and press **Ctrl + T** to convert the range into a proper table.
💬 Example row: "Acme Studio | INV-1042 | 1 March 2026 | 31 March 2026 | 1200 | Pending"
You'll know it worked when you can click the filter arrow on the Client column and see the names you just typed.

## Step 4 — Ask Copilot for the Days Overdue formula
Click into the cell in row 2 of the **Days Overdue** column so Copilot knows where to start. In the chat panel, type a request asking for a formula that calculates how late each invoice is. Copilot usually shows the formula first — read it and check it mentions "TODAY" and the Due Date column. If it looks right, click **Insert** and the formula appears, then **auto-fills down** the column. If it looks wrong — wrong column, missing parentheses, weird logic — ask Copilot to rewrite it. Never trust a formula you can't explain in plain English.
💬 Example: "In the Days Overdue column, write a formula that subtracts the Due Date from TODAY(). Show 0 if the date isn't past yet."
You'll know it worked when numbers like **5**, **12**, or **0** appear in the column, with overdue rows showing positive numbers.

## Step 5 — Ask Copilot to color-code the overdue rows
Click anywhere in your data first, so the formatting applies to the whole table. In the chat panel, ask Copilot to apply **conditional formatting** (rules that colour cells automatically based on their value) using the Days Overdue column. Copilot usually shows a preview of which cells will be highlighted before applying — confirm and the formatting sticks. If the prompt doesn't work, do it manually: select the Days Overdue column, go to **Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cell Rules → Greater Than**, enter **7** for red, then repeat with **Between 1 and 7** for yellow.
💬 Example: "Highlight rows red where Days Overdue is more than 7, and yellow where it's between 1 and 7."
You'll know it worked when overdue rows visibly stand out — red for the very late ones, yellow for the almost-late ones.

## Step 6 — Save, sort, and send reminders yourself
Press **Ctrl + S** (Windows) or **⌘ + S** (Mac) and pick a OneDrive or local location to save your tracker. It's ready to use. Here's the honest limit: **Copilot in Excel cannot send emails automatically.** For the actual nudge, you'll still open Outlook or Gmail, filter your tracker by the red rows, and send a polite follow-up yourself. If you want automatic email reminders later, you'd need a separate tool — Power Automate, a dedicated invoicing app, or a workflow service — which is beyond what Excel's Copilot does today.
💬 Example: filter the table by Status "Overdue" to see your chase list in one click.
You'll know it worked when you can re-open the file tomorrow, sort by Days Overdue, and instantly see who to chase first.

## Common mistakes
- **Trusting a formula you didn't read.** Copilot writes decent formulas but they sometimes point at the wrong column, miss parentheses, or use a different date logic. Always click the cell and read the formula in the formula bar before trusting the result. If it looks suspicious, ask Copilot to explain it in plain English, or rewrite the prompt.
- **Skipping the plan check.** If the Copilot button never appears, it's almost always because the account doesn't have Copilot enabled. Confirm your Microsoft 365 plan includes Copilot before troubleshooting anything else — that one check saves an hour of frustration.
- **Typing dates as text.** If you type "31 March" without a year, Excel may store it as text and your formulas will break silently. Always include the year, and confirm the column header shows the word "Date" formatting.

## What this means for you
- **If you run a small business or freelance:** You now have a low-effort way to see your cash-flow picture at a glance, and a polite way to know exactly who to chase on Monday morning.
- **If you manage a team or bookkeep for someone else:** This tracker becomes a shared template — anyone with the right Microsoft 365 plan can use it, and the formulas don't need to be rebuilt each time.
- **If you're just getting started:** The simplest first move is to copy the example prompt in Step 2 exactly, then swap in your real column names if you need to.

## Try it now
Open a blank Excel workbook, click the Copilot button, and paste this exact prompt: **"Create a table with columns: Client, Invoice Number, Invoice Date, Due Date, Amount, Status, Days Overdue."** See what Copilot proposes before you change anything — that's the fastest way to feel how it works.
